title: Same hours, different calendar
hook: Three hours in one block or across three days: what changes a month later?

knows: reading short labels and comparing simple counts
doesNotKnow: Separate the research-supported spacing effect from invented memory curves.

misconception: Equal study hours imply equal long-term recall regardless of calendar.
objective: Separate the research-supported spacing effect from invented memory curves.

claims.text: Scenario, hook and prediction: Three hours in one block or across three days: what changes a month later? For equal study time, which plan generally supports longer-term verbal recall? Correct option: Distributed sessions. All fixture labels, example words, dates, task durations and file fields are stipulated exercise data.
claims.source: Explicit exercise fixture in src/lib/lifehacks/studyCatalog.ts and pure rules in studyModels.ts. All times, sizes, deadlines and outcomes describe this exercise only; no empirical productivity or learning effect is inferred.

claims.text: Research on verbal recall supports distributed practice. The curves illustrate that idea; they do not predict your memory.
claims.source: Cepeda et al. (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks, Psychological Bulletin132(3),354–380, DOI10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354, author abstract via https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/ retrieved2026-10-13; 839 assessments in317 experiments. Rawson & Kintsch(2005), Rereading Effects Depend on Time of Test, JEP97(1),70–80, DOI10.1037/0022-0663.97.1.70, author abstract search record https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ688037 retrieved2026-10-13 (direct page timed out). Retrieval line supported separately by Roediger & Karpicke(2006), Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science 17(3),249–255, DOI10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x; publisher abstract retrieved 2026-10-13: https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x/ . Prose-passage experiments found delayed retention advantages for retrieval over restudy. This short exercise does not establish that effect for the learner.

claims.text: Every displayed result is computed from the visible exercise state: spacing. Illustrative curves; not personal memory predictions. The reveal reports this same state and never translates its score into a personal productivity or memory benefit.
claims.source: src/lib/lifehacks/studyModels.ts and src/components/lifehacks/StudyLesson.tsx, spaced-beats-cram fixture in src/lib/lifehacks/studyCatalog.ts. Stage rules: cram=exp(-day/7), distributed=exp(-day/18); illustrative parameters, not fitted data. Marker visits gate the reveal; three sessions on days-2,-1,0 are calendar markers, not fitted review boosts. Future decay curves, scrub marker and retention-point markers are not rendered before prediction; only neutral stipulated calendars and chart axes are shown while locked.

claims.text: Recall question answer and rationale: Distributed sessions. Research on verbal recall supports distributed practice. The curves illustrate that idea; they do not predict your memory.

Retrieval line supported separately by Roediger & Karpicke(2006), Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science 17(3),249–255, DOI10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x; publisher abstract retrieved 2026-10-13: https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x/ . Prose-passage experiments found delayed retention advantages for retrieval over restudy. This short exercise does not establish that effect for the learner.

claims.text: Massed rereading can perform better on an immediate test while distributed rereading can perform better on a delayed test; this does not establish the model curves or next-morning performance.
claims.source: Rawson & Kintsch(2005) author abstract via ERIC EJ688037. Retrieval is supported separately by Roediger & Karpicke(2006), publisher abstract. The lesson does not use Cepeda2006 as evidence for immediate-test reversal.
